accroche: For sixty-six years, giving a gift in public could mean prison in Canada.
contenu_vulgarise:
Among the peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast (Kwakwaka'wakw, Tsimshian, Haida, among others), the potlatch is a ceremony in which a chief or a family asserts its rank by publicly distributing, or even destroying, a large quantity of goods: blankets, engraved coppers, food. The more generous the gift, the higher the giver's status rises. In this system, wealth is not measured by what you keep. It is measured by what you give away.

## A Law Against a Ceremony

On April 19, 1884, the Canadian government amended the Indian Act to write in, effective January 1, 1885, an outright ban on the potlatch: anyone who took part in it or helped celebrate it was guilty of an offense, punishable by prison. The official reason came down to one word: assimilation. The ceremony was said to stand in its way. Administrators and missionaries saw it as wasteful, contrary to Christianity as well as to the accumulation of goods; Prime Minister John A. Macdonald wanted to put an end to the tribal system.

The ban went largely unenforced for decades. On December 25, 1921, Chief Dan Cranmer held at Village Island the largest potlatch ever recorded on the Northwest Coast: some three hundred people attended. The Indian Affairs agent and the police intervened only after the ceremony. Forty-five people were charged; twenty-two received suspended sentences in exchange for handing over their ritual objects (masks, headdresses, rattles), and twenty were taken in 1922 to Oakalla prison, near Vancouver. More than six hundred pieces were confiscated.

The German-American anthropologist Franz Boas, who devoted part of his career to documenting Kwakwaka'wakw culture, publicly opposed the law. With the help of his Indigenous assistant, he even went so far as to take part in a potlatch himself, fully aware of the legal risk. The law was not repealed until 1951; the first potlatch to be legal again took place the following year in Victoria, led by the Kwakwaka'wakw chief Mungo Martin.

## What This Shifts

The paradox deserves to be followed through to the end: a state judged a gift dangerous enough to be made to disappear by force. The potlatch was disturbing precisely because it organized an economy and a social hierarchy independent of those the colonial power was trying to impose. Redistribution played there the role that accumulation plays elsewhere.

The confiscated regalia, scattered among national museums, private collectors, and foreign institutions (from Ottawa and Toronto to New York and the United Kingdom), were the subject, beginning in the 1970s, of a long campaign of return to the Kwakwaka'wakw communities, rebuilding piece by piece a memory that the ban had sought to erase.

repere.texte: The law took effect on January 1, 1885, and was not repealed until 1951: sixty-six years of legal prohibition, marked by the forty-five charges that followed the potlatch given by Dan Cranmer at Village Island on December 25, 1921.
repere.source: U'mista Cultural Society; The Canadian Encyclopedia

carte.punch: Giving a gift in public could mean prison.
carte.idee: From 1885 to 1951, Canada banned by law the potlatch, a ceremony in which people assert their rank by giving away their wealth. Forty-five people were charged for holding one at Christmas 1921; twenty went to prison.

quiz.question: Why did the Canadian government ban the potlatch in 1885?
choix: To protect participants from frequent shipwrecks
Because it stood in the way of the assimilation of Indigenous peoples
To preserve the regalia in national museums
Because the Kwakwaka'wakw themselves asked for it
quiz.explication: The official reason the government gave was that the potlatch prevented the assimilation of Indigenous peoples. The regalia were not seized in order to be preserved. They were wrested away in exchange for suspended sentences, and no community ever asked for this ban.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In the potlatch, how is the rank of the person giving it measured?
choix: By the quantity of goods his family manages to accumulate
By the quantity of goods he distributes or destroys in public
By the number of engraved coppers received from neighboring families
By the extent of the fishing grounds his clan controls
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The potlatch reverses the ordinary measure of wealth: status comes from what you give. The more generous the distribution, the higher the giver's rank rises.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happened to the participants in Dan Cranmer's potlatch?
choix: The police intervened during the ceremony to interrupt it
Those charged were acquitted for lack of an applicable legal text
Forty-five people were charged, and twenty went to prison
Only Chief Dan Cranmer was convicted, with a suspended sentence
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Indian Affairs agent and the police intervened only after the ceremony. Of the forty-five people charged, twenty-two received suspended sentences by handing over their ritual objects, and twenty were taken in 1922 to Oakalla prison.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What position did the anthropologist Franz Boas take on this law?
choix: He publicly opposed it and took part in a potlatch himself
He supported it, seeing a chance to collect ritual objects
He stayed silent to preserve his access to his fieldwork
He proposed replacing it with a permit issued case by case
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Boas had devoted part of his career to documenting Kwakwaka'wakw culture. He publicly opposed the ban, and he took part in a potlatch fully aware of the legal risk, with the help of his Indigenous assistant.
